title: A Successful Space Race Needs More than “Competitive Supremacy”
summary:
The final frontier must be mutually beneficial for both US and Allies to be sustainable

While the demand for digital sovereignty continues to accelerate, driven by geopolitics and strategic necessity, recent announcements about space supremacy, the unqualified success of Artemis and massive industry growth have created what can only be described as excitement beyond any recent experience. The vision, potential addressable markets, technological innovation, and the challenges and opportunities ahead are significant and possibly already past the point of regulation.

But it does raise a profound question: how can the very nature of space as a highly contested domain align with the sovereign interests of both the US and its Allies? And why must these interests be protected for the benefit of the Alliance?

Given the existential nature of the outcomes, we cannot leave the question purely to fate.

title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
summary:
Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll

Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.

As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.

Given that the US-China AI arms race forms the backdrop of the upheaval at Nvidia, you can't understand Jensen Huang's resignation without considering geopolitical and global economic conditions. title: Not All Those Who Wander Are Lost album review – Anna Lapwood journeys to middle earth
summary:
Lapwood/Nidaros Cathedral Girls’ Choir
(Sony)
Lapwood has turned Howard Shore’s film score into an impressive full-blown organ symphony

When a fan requested she play Concerning Hobbits from The Lord of the Rings, little did Anna Lapwood imagine that she would go on to spend a year turning Howard Shore’s leitmotif-led soundtrack into a full-blown organ symphony. Remarkably, she transcribed all but one segment by ear, a feat in itself. That she manages to tell the story chronologically over a 38-minute, three-movement span is equally impressive.

But wait, there’s more. title: Midnight Diner: Netflix just dropped its most beautiful show in years … and it’s barely been noticed
summary:
Disarmingly thoughtful stillness is the order of the day in the latest season of this Japanese show about a Tokyo eatery. What a shame it feels buried under other content

The first time we see the Master (Kaoru Kobayashi) in the sixth season of Midnight Diner, he cuts a curiously morose figure. His usually bustling establishment – open from midnight to 7am – is empty. No one, he notes, will come: Covid-19 keeps them at home. An ironic start for a drama arriving after a seven-year absence, delayed in part by uncertainty over the pandemic’s impact on small eateries.

The show’s return isn’t a shock. Based on Yarō Abe’s long-running manga, it has been a TV fixture in Japan since 2009. Netflix has just quietly released it, buried by the platform’s seeming aversion to marketing non-English series, which has swallowed reams of remarkable Japanese television.

title: ‘I was nervous before my solo stay in a remote Scottish Highlands cabin – but the solitude is glorious’

Just a few minutes earlier, I had been scuffing my feet in the sand by the loch shore, watching as the clouds draped themselves across the top of the Grampians. In the absence of other people, Loch Laidon, silvery in the half-light, had been mine to enjoy; in the woods, however, my solitude feels unnerving.

I turned 40 a few years ago. For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful. They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health.

I place a lot of importance on gift giving. It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you. To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care.

title: Indigenous students retrace Lewis and Clark’s historic journey: ‘We can’t protect what we cannot see’

In 1804, when Thomas Jefferson dispatched Meriwether Lewis and William Clark and their Corps of Discovery to explore the newly acquired land west of the Mississippi, the president’s primary aim was political: Americans needed to establish presence, power and trade routes in these territories before the Europeans beat them to it.

But Jefferson, an ardent naturalist, had a secondary agenda. He ordered that the expedition also survey the flora and fauna of these landscapes. On their two-year jaunt across the western half of the country, Lewis and Clark kept meticulous journals of the animals and plants they encountered: bison, horned lizards, sage grouse, prairie dogs, wild licorice and catfish, among them. These observations were pivotal in shaping an early understanding of North American biodiversity.

Ask the average American to name an elite US fighting force, and they might kick off with the Rangers or the Seals. But during the Vietnam war, a specialized patrol of army volunteers became critical to the US military effort.

Known as long-range reconnaissance patrols, or LRRPs, these small teams of six to eight soldiers were dropped behind enemy lines to track supply routes and hostile positions, sometimes for days at a time. Stealth was essential. Their job was to identify targets and call in the cavalry, usually in the form of airstrikes, while avoiding direct engagement with enemy forces to preserve their cover.

A rough halt hewn out of the mountainside, with no ticket office, no waiting room, no sign of human habitation – just a single platform in the wilderness. On the far side of the track, a shimmering turquoise lake flanked by pine forests. Ahead – the only way out – a rocky trail snaking up the limestone cliff.

My husband and I had first strayed into this western corner of Catalonia – Pallars Jussà – on our honeymoon road trip 21 years earlier. Seduced by its dramatic landscape of canyons, lakes, crumbling ruins and the formidable Noguera Pallaresa river thundering south from the Pyrenees, we had vowed to return one day.
